title: Design Distributed Caching for ASP.NET Core
description: Use Redis, SQL Server cache, or in-memory cache to scale ASP.NET Core applications under high load.

data.text: Your API repeatedly queries the same product catalog data. Database load is growing. Design a caching layer that works across multiple server instances.
Fast but local to a single server. Does not share state across instances. Good for single-instance apps or data that does not need to be consistent across servers.

data.title: In-Memory Cache Registration

data.text: Shared across all instances. Survives app restarts. Supports expiration, pub/sub, and clustering. Best choice for multi-instance deployments.

data.title: Redis Distributed Cache

data.text: Choose the right strategy based on read/write ratio and consistency requirements.

data.title: Caching Strategies
items: **Cache-Aside**: App checks cache first, falls back to DB, then populates cache. Most common pattern.
**Write-Through**: App writes to cache and DB simultaneously. Stronger consistency but more complex.
**Write-Behind**: App writes to cache, cache asynchronously flushes to DB. Fast but risk of data loss.
**Refresh-Ahead**: Proactively refresh cache before expiration. Good for hot data.

data.title: Cache Invalidation
data.text: The hardest part of caching is knowing when to remove stale data. Use cache keys with version segments, TTLs, and explicit invalidation on writes.

data.title: Cache Key Versioning
Key Takeaways
points: Use Redis for multi-instance apps requiring shared cache state
IMemoryCache is faster but local to a single server
Cache-Aside is the simplest and most common pattern
Always set TTLs to prevent stale data from living forever
Version your cache keys to make invalidation manageable
data.takeaway: Caching is one of the most effective ways to scale ASP.NET Core, but choose the right strategy for your consistency and deployment needs.
